Gina Martin Adams: Most global bond markets have struggled somewhat as of late, but the move has been less broad in emerging markets relative to developed markets.  Over the last year, 11 of the 15 emerging markets we track showed an increase in 10-year yield, while all 20 developed markets saw 10-year yields rise.  

Indeed, the last several years of repricing in global bond markets has been heavily centered on developed markets, and not just because developed market 10-year yields were near zero in the pandemic and have repriced rapidly.
...
The spread compression between EM and DM debt has been so extreme that by at least one measure, 10-year emerging market sovereign yields are now lower than 10-year developed market sovereign yields for the first time in our records. On a debt-weighted basis, emerging market 10-year sovereign debt is yielding 4.47%, slightly less than developed market sovereign debt, yielding 4.58%.

https://t.co/ZPaDcmNXgB

BREAKING: Malaysia's exports surged +54.5% YoY in September, to a record $52.7 billion, their largest YoY increase since April 2021.

Malaysia’s exports have now seen above +35.0% YoY growth for 6 consecutive months, the longest such streak since the 1970s.

The surge has been driven by manufactured goods, which rose +58.6% YoY and accounted for 89.1% of total exports.

Electrical and electronic product exports rose +69.2% YoY amid strong global demand for AI-related products.

Exports surged +175.2% to Taiwan, +89.9% to the US, +50.4% to Singapore, +35.3% to the EU, and +22.1% to China.

The global AI investment boom is driving an unprecedented surge in Asian trade.

Gold stocks have rarely been this oversold.

~92% of stocks in the gold miners ETF, $GDX, are now trading below their 50-day moving average, the highest proportion since late July.

This figure has risen +80 percentage points in just 21 sessions.

Furthermore, 90% of stocks in $GDX are trading below their 200-day moving average, the highest proportion in 3 months.

Similar setups occurred in March 2024 and December 2024.

In the following month, $GDX rallied +21.5% and +15.4%, respectively.

History suggests the selloff in gold miners is nearing exhaustion.

BREAKING: The Memory ETF, $DRAM, has posted -$2.0 billion in outflows so far in October, putting the fund on track for its largest monthly withdrawal since launching on April 2nd.

This would also mark its 3rd consecutive monthly outflow, following -$1.6 billion in September and -$400 million in August.

Last week alone, $DRAM saw -$105 million in outflows, its 9th consecutive weekly withdrawal.

As a result, the fund is down -23% month-to-date, trading near its lowest level since early May.

Yet, $DRAM is still up +70% since inception, after recording a +190% gain in mid-June.

Meanwhile, the 2x leveraged long Memory ETF, $RAM, is down -66% since its June 24th debut.

The memory chip trade has seen a major pullback.

🚨🇫🇷 France is now borrowing at more than 5% over 10 years and consequences could be far more significant than markets currently anticipate - FT

📈 Despite rising bond yields, France remains far from a sovereign debt crisis but the spread between French and German 10-year bonds is hovering around 170 basis points. Moreover, when we convert five-year sovereign yields into US dollars using cross-currency swaps, stripping out much of the difference in monetary policy expectations, French debt shows a synthetic yield above 6% compared with 5% for the US. Even though, this is not the rate at which France actually borrows, it reveals a significant deterioration in the compensation investors demand to hold French government debt.

💰 With an average debt maturity of more than eight years, France benefits from a substantial buffer as higher interest rates do not immediately affect the entire outstanding debt stock. However, this buffer only delays the problem and doesn't eliminate it. The French government's interest bill is expected to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027. With €340 billion in medium- and long-term bond issuance planned for 2027, net of buybacks, a sustained 100-basis-point increase in borrowing costs could translate into several billion euros in additional annualized interest expenses on new issuance alone. If rates remain elevated long enough, this could structurally weaken France's public finances.

🇪🇺 France's situation remains nowhere near the European sovereign debt crisis of 2011–2012, when Greek bond spreads reached several thousand basis points. However, France doesn't need to experience a Greek-style crisis to suffer a major deterioration in debt sustainability. Unlike the US, whose interest burden as a share of GDP is actually higher, France does not independently control its monetary policy. Some argue that worsening French economic conditions would push the ECB to act but there is no guarantee that a confidence crisis specific to France would trigger monetary easing across the entire eurozone.

⚠️ When borrowing costs remain elevated while economic growth is weak and primary deficits persist, stabilizing public debt requires fiscal adjustments. Those adjustments can themselves weigh on economic growth making fiscal consolidation even harder. France still has full access to capital markets and government bond auctions continue to attract investors but we may face a fiscal credibility crisis that gradually becomes entrenched.

➡️ I believe the main risk is that investors continue to finance France at a price that makes its fiscal trajectory increasingly difficult to sustain, and that doesn't require a spectacular sovereign debt crisis.

*FT link: https://t.co/14FKUfN3nC
